title: Are discrete logarithms in prime fields in randomized polynomial time?
formal: Is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every prime p, every generator g of the multiplicative group Fₚ*, and every h∈Fₚ*, returns the unique integer x∈{0,…,p−2} satisfying gˣ≡h (mod p), with probability at least 2/3 and worst-case running time polynomial in log₂p?
definitions: The input consists of ordinary binary integers (p,g,h), with p prime and 1≤g,h≤p−1, promised that g has multiplicative order p−1. Set n=⌈log₂(p+1)⌉; the total input length is Θ(n). A single probabilistic Turing machine must use at most C(n+1)^c bit operations on every random tape, for fixed constants C,c independent of p,g,h. It may output failure on unsuccessful runs. Success probability is over its own independent fair random bits and must be at least 2/3 separately on every promised input. Its only input is (p,g,h): no factorization of p−1, precomputed logarithm table, advice, special-form description of p, or oracle is supplied. Any preprocessing it performs counts in its runtime. The algorithm may exploit the ordinary integer encoding and all efficiently computable arithmetic modulo p; it is not restricted to generic group operations. The group is multiplication of nonzero residues, not an elliptic-curve group or the additive group. For p=2 the only logarithm is x=0.
answer_criterion: Give and prove a classical algorithm with the specified uniform polynomial worst-case time and per-instance success guarantee, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A generic-group lower bound, a fast algorithm for a restricted family of primes, a quantum algorithm, or a polynomial bound in p rather than log p does not settle the question.
context:
Computing gˣ mod p is efficient by repeated squaring, even when x is given in binary and is as large as p−2. The inverse problem asks which exponent produced a residue. A polynomial-time solution would remove the computational asymmetry used in finite-field discrete-logarithm cryptography. It would also solve the corresponding computational Diffie–Hellman problem by recovering an exponent, although hardness of discrete logarithms alone does not establish every stronger security assumption.

A proposed answer is easy to verify: check the exponent range and compute gˣ mod p. Consequently a bounded-error polynomial algorithm could be repeated until a verified answer is obtained, giving expected polynomial time with no incorrect output. Conversely, a verified expected-polynomial-time solver can be truncated and repeated to obtain constant success within a polynomial budget. This makes the fixed runtime convention compatible with the usual Las Vegas formulation.

The number field sieve exploits arithmetic structure that generic group algorithms cannot see. It gathers multiplicative relations among suitably smooth objects, solves a large linear system, and reduces an individual target to the resulting logarithms. Its usual large-characteristic complexity estimates have the heuristic subexponential form exp(O((ln p)^{1/3}(ln ln p)^{2/3})). This grows faster than every polynomial in the bit length.

Generic lower bounds do not settle the concrete prime-field problem. Shoup proves a square-root barrier in the size of the largest prime factor of a group’s order when elements are accessed through an abstract random encoding. The present algorithm receives actual residues and can use their number-theoretic structure, as the sieve already does. A proof against the oracle model cannot simply be transferred to this richer interface.

The field regime is crucial. Kleinjung and Wesolowski give a rigorous expected-time bound (p·d)^{2log₂d+O(1)} for discrete logarithms in F_{p^d}. For fixed p and growing extension degree d this is quasipolynomial in the input size. For prime fields d=1 and growing p, that expression is merely polynomial in p, which is exponential in its binary length. Their breakthrough therefore leaves this question open.

Later sieve work also studies how preprocessing can be shared across targets and across fields. The Discrete Logarithm Factory paper develops such improvements, especially for non-prime fields, and distinguishes the cost of a target logarithm from the cost of building reusable data. Here all preprocessing is charged to the algorithm on a single input, so a cheap online lookup after a very expensive table construction is insufficient.
why: A fundamental inversion problem in computational number theory and a central candidate for separating efficient classical from quantum computation. Its resolution would clarify which arithmetic structure can overcome generic group barriers and would reshape finite-field cryptographic assumptions.

importance.reason: One of the principal unresolved number-theoretic algorithmic problems, with direct connections to cryptography, index calculus, and quantum speedups.

progress.text: Number-field-sieve methods give heuristic subexponential algorithms for prime-field discrete logarithms; their arithmetic relations go beyond the generic group model.
Shor gives quantum polynomial-time algorithms for factoring and discrete logarithms. The classical requirement in this question is essential.
Shoup proves square-root lower bounds for generic group algorithms, parameterized by the largest prime factor of the group order. These are model-restricted lower bounds.
Kleinjung and Wesolowski prove quasipolynomial expected time for fixed-characteristic finite fields. Their theorem does not give polynomial time in log p for the prime-field family.

Al Aswad, Thomé, and Pierrot develop the Discrete Logarithm Factory approach to sharing sieve computations, while continuing to describe NFS variants as the leading methods outside small characteristic.

status_note: Open in the cited computational-number-theory literature; checked through 10 September 2026. No uniform classical polynomial-in-log-p solver or unrestricted exclusion was found. The card keeps heuristic sieve analyses, fixed-characteristic extension fields, reusable preprocessing, and quantum algorithms separate.
